newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain, Ireland, pledge to back N.Ireland talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland, pledge to back N.Ireland talks.

text.p: Britain and Ireland promised on Thursday to breathe new life into Northern Ireland peace talks after months of rising tension fuelled by sectarian divisions and feuds in Protestant Loyalist groups. Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said the two governments, which are sponsoring the troubled negotiations, were determined to "put new momentum into the multi-party talks" which resume in Belfast next Monday. He was speaking after two hours of talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, amid concern that a feud in Northern Ireland's Loyalist community threatens to put fresh strain on the negotiations. "We want to encourage all the parties to recognise that the talking process is the only way forward. Underlying everything is a very strong belief throughout Northern Ireland that talking must be given a chance," Mayhew said.
Both men said it was likely that Loyalist political groups at the talks faced calls for their expulsion from other parties because of a death threat against a militant Loyalist called Billy Wright.
Wright, a convicted activist, was ordered by Protestant Loyalist militia to leave the province by midnight last Saturday for challenging the policies being pursued at the talks by Loyalist parties.

The issue has escalated from a regional sideshow based around Wright's home town of Portadown, south of Belfast, into a direct challenge to the authority of the Loyalist parties to speak for Protestants who want the province to remain British.

Spring told Irish RTE radio that public backing for Wright marked a continuation of militant Protestant opposition to the peace talks which exploded over the summer in Protestant parades and riots across the province.
"I would see it as an unfortunate continuation of the deterioration of the situation which took place in the summer," Spring said.

On Wednesday night thousands of people attended a rally in support of Wright, who has been convicted of security offences and is said by security sources to be close to the leadership of one faction of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force guerrillas.

Wright was feted like a hero at the rally and told his supporters he opposed the policies of Loyalist parties taking part in the peace talks because the negotiations were aimed at ending British rule of Northern Ireland.
"I will not become part of a process that is designed to ease our people into a united Ireland," said Wright. "I am living through the death of our nation and the destruction of our way of life."

The British and Irish governments have hinted that two small parties representing Loyalist militia, the Progressive Unionist Party and Ulster Democratic Party, might be removed from the talks unless the death threat against Wright is lifted.
They have said that all participants in the negotiations have to abide by principles of non-violence and that the threats against Wright are incompatible with democracy.
Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA guerrillas fighting British rule of the province, has been barred from the talks because of the guerrillas' failure to reinstate a ceasefire they broke in February.

The removal of the hard-line Loyalist parties would leave only established mainstream political groups at the talks who have been unable to make any headway towards a Northern Ireland settlement for 27 years.
